sections.tagline: The offered purpose controls the policy exclusion.

points.title: Later repairs
points.text: 407 bars subsequent measures to prove negligence, culpable conduct, product/design defect, or need for warning. Other purposes include disputed ownership, control, or feasibility, and appropriate impeachment. Earlier precautions and earlier incidents raise different issues.

points.title: Settlement and treatment payments
points.text: 408 bars compromise offers and negotiation statements about a disputed claim for specified liability, amount, and contradiction-impeachment purposes, with defined other uses and an important public-office criminal-case qualification. 409 bars offers/payment of medical expenses to prove liability but does not independently protect accompanying admissions.

points.title: Insurance
points.text: 411 bars liability insurance or its absence to prove negligence or wrongful action; other relevant purposes include agency, ownership, control, or bias. Establish genuine relevance and apply 403 rather than treating an exception label as automatic admission.

sections.example: After a visitor falls, a museum installs a rail. It also offers medical expenses and says, “We forgot the inspection.” Separate the later repair, the payment offer, and the accompanying statement; determine whether a disputed claim and negotiations existed.
tips: State the precise offered purpose and identify the facts needed for this rule’s foundation.
Change one fact in the worked example and explain which requirement changes the result.

terms.definition: A post-event action that would have made the harm less likely.
A claim contested as to validity or amount, central to Rule 408.
Practical ability to take a precaution, an allowed 407 purpose when disputed.

sections.comicCaption: Detective: “The offered purpose controls the policy exclusion.” Advocate: “Later repairs: 407 bars subsequent measures to prove negligence, culpable conduct, product/design defect, or need for warning. ”

writtenPractice.prompt: A cafe adds a nonslip mat after a fall, offers to pay the customer’s medical expenses, and says “we left grease on the floor.” It later disputes whether any mat could physically fit the location.
writtenPractice.analysis: 407 generally excludes the later mat to prove negligence, but disputed feasibility can support a limited other-purpose use. 409 protects the medical-payment offer for liability use, not automatically the accompanying fault admission. If communications occur in negotiations about a disputed claim, analyze 408 separately.
writtenPractice.variation: Make feasibility conceded and identify whether the mat has any other permissible, genuinely relevant purpose.

sections.title: Plea discussions & completeness
sections.tagline: Context may need to arrive with the excerpt.

points.title: Protected plea material
points.text: Rule 410 protects withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, qualifying plea-proceeding statements, and plea discussions with a prosecuting attorney resulting in no plea or a later-withdrawn plea, when offered against the participating defendant. An ordinary police confession is not automatically a plea discussion.

points.title: Exceptions and waiver
points.text: 410 includes a contextual fairness exception and specified perjury/false-statement use under oath, on the record, and with counsel. Mezzanatto permits certain waivers; read the actual waiver and its scope rather than assuming every negotiation is protected or fully waived.

points.title: Current completeness rule
points.text: 106 covers all statements, including unrecorded oral statements. An adverse party may require contemporaneous introduction of another part or statement that fairness requires, over a hearsay objection. It supplies necessary context, not a right to admit every favorable remark.

sections.example: A recording is played as “I took the cash,” cutting off “from my own account with the manager’s permission.” Consider contemporaneous completion. Separately, a prosecutor’s plea meeting and an officer’s casual bargaining conversation need different Rule 410 analysis.
tips: State the precise offered purpose and identify the facts needed for this rule’s foundation.
Change one fact in the worked example and explain which requirement changes the result.

terms.definition: A negotiation with the prosecuting attorney meeting Rule 410’s conditions.
Contemporaneous contextual material necessary to prevent a misleading partial statement.
An intentional relinquishment evaluated according to its enforceable scope.

sections.comicCaption: Detective: “Context may need to arrive with the excerpt.” Advocate: “Protected plea material: Rule 410 protects withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, qualifying plea-proceeding statements, and plea discussions with a prosecuting attorney resulting in no plea or a later-withdrawn plea, when offered against the participating defendant. ”

writtenPractice.prompt: Counsel offers only “I moved the funds” from an oral account whose next words are “after the owner authorized the transfer.” The opponent wants completion immediately. Separately, the defendant offered an officer cooperation in exchange for leniency without involving a prosecutor.
writtenPractice.analysis: 106 can require necessary contemporaneous context, including oral statements and over a hearsay objection. It does not admit unrelated favorable material. An officer conversation is not automatically protected under 410’s prosecuting-attorney discussion provision; establish the actual speaker and negotiating authority rather than assume it.
writtenPractice.variation: Add a prosecutor-led plea meeting and compare the separate 410 conditions.

sections.title: Privileges: governing law, holder & confidential purpose
sections.tagline: Secrecy alone does not create a privilege.

points.title: Which law?
points.text: Rule 501 uses federal common law, shaped by reason and experience, except as otherwise provided. In a civil case, state law governs privilege for a claim or defense whose rule of decision comes from state law. Identify the governing issue before choosing a privilege.

points.title: Who holds it?
points.text: Attorney-client protection generally covers confidential communications for obtaining or providing legal advice; it protects communications, not underlying facts. The client ordinarily holds it. Business advice, a copied lawyer, or confidentiality alone does not establish it.

points.title: Other privileges
points.text: Jaffee recognizes confidential psychotherapist-patient communications, including licensed clinical social workers, under federal law. Spousal testimonial and confidential-communication privileges are distinct, with different holders and limits. Work product comes from separate procedural protections.

sections.example: A manager forwards ordinary sales figures to company counsel and asks for no legal advice. A different message requests confidential legal guidance. Determine governing law, the claimed privilege’s elements, and who can assert or waive it.
tips: State the precise offered purpose and identify the facts needed for this rule’s foundation.
Change one fact in the worked example and explain which requirement changes the result.

terms.definition: The person legally entitled to assert or waive the protection.
The professional-advice purpose required by attorney-client privilege.
Information that does not become privileged merely because someone later tells a lawyer.

sections.comicCaption: Detective: “Secrecy alone does not create a privilege.” Advocate: “Which law?: Rule 501 uses federal common law, shaped by reason and experience, except as otherwise provided. ”

writtenPractice.prompt: An executive emails counsel a legal question and attaches a preexisting inventory spreadsheet. A therapist separately records confidential treatment discussions with the executive. What is protected and under what law?
writtenPractice.analysis: Choose federal or state privilege law under 501 for the relevant claims. The confidential legal-advice communication may be privileged; attaching a preexisting business document does not automatically cloak the spreadsheet itself. Under federal law, Jaffee protects qualifying confidential psychotherapeutic communications, including with licensed clinical social workers.
writtenPractice.variation: Add unrelated outsiders to the legal email and examine whether confidentiality and purpose remain.

sections.title: Waiver, clawback & privilege policy
sections.tagline: Protect the communication and respond promptly to mistakes.

points.title: Purpose and disclosure
points.text: A conversation with a friend who happens to be clergy or a lawyer does not automatically meet the professional-purpose requirement. Voluntary disclosure and putting advice at issue can waive privilege; distinguish privilege from broader ethical confidentiality.

points.title: Inadvertent disclosure
points.text: Under 502(b), an inadvertent disclosure in a federal proceeding or to a federal office/agency avoids waiver if reasonable preventive steps were taken and reasonable steps promptly rectify the error. Carmody focuses on the actual review and response, not perfection.

points.title: Orders and scope
points.text: 502(a) limits subject-matter waiver to defined intentional-disclosure circumstances and fairness. A 502(d) order can protect against waiver in other federal or state proceedings; a 502(e) party agreement alone binds only the parties unless incorporated in an order. Work-product protection remains distinct from privilege.

sections.example: A reviewed production accidentally includes a legal memo. Counsel demands return as soon as it is used, follows up, and promptly seeks a ruling. Contrast an office that intentionally publishes the memo or waits after learning of disclosure.
tips: State the precise offered purpose and identify the facts needed for this rule’s foundation.
Change one fact in the worked example and explain which requirement changes the result.

terms.definition: Seeking return or protected treatment of mistakenly disclosed material.
Fairness-based extension beyond the disclosed communication under defined conditions.
A court order protecting against waiver beyond the parties’ private agreement.

sections.comicCaption: Detective: “Protect the communication and respond promptly to mistakes.” Advocate: “Purpose and disclosure: A conversation with a friend who happens to be clergy or a lawyer does not automatically meet the professional-purpose requirement. ”

writtenPractice.prompt: A legal memo is mistakenly included in federal discovery after documented review. Counsel learns of it and waits three months before seeking return. The parties have only a private clawback agreement.
writtenPractice.analysis: Inadvertence and reasonable prevention do not suffice if prompt reasonable correction is missing under 502(b). A 502(e) agreement ordinarily binds only its parties unless incorporated in an order; a 502(d) order has different effects. Determine when counsel learned and what actions followed; do not treat a privilege label as dispositive.
writtenPractice.variation: Replace the delay with an immediate request, follow-up, and prompt motion, then compare Carmody.

sections.title: Foundations, statutory interpretation & trial procedure
sections.tagline: Start with the text and the proceeding.

points.title: The rules as enacted law
points.text: Begin with the rule’s text, read its structure, and use Advisory Committee Notes and relevant legislative history to resolve uncertainty. Rule 102 states interpretive purposes; it does not authorize ignoring a specific exclusion.

points.title: Scope of the rules
points.text: 1101 applies the rules to specified federal courts and proceedings, with important exceptions including grand jury, sentencing, and 104(a) admissibility fact determinations. Privilege rules continue to apply where the other evidence rules do not.

points.title: Preserve and limit
points.text: Use a timely specific objection or offer of proof under 103. Distinguish judge-decided 104(a) admissibility questions from 104(b) conditional relevance. Under 105, seek a limiting instruction when evidence is admissible for one purpose or party but not another.

sections.example: At sentencing, counsel objects that a report is hearsay. First ask whether the ordinary evidence rules govern that proceeding, then examine other applicable protections. At trial, the same report requires an ordinary admissibility analysis.
tips: State the precise offered purpose and identify the facts needed for this rule’s foundation.
Change one fact in the worked example and explain which requirement changes the result.

terms.definition: The enacted language that starts the interpretation.
Interpretive background accompanying a rule or amendment.
Directions restricting the jury’s use of evidence to its permitted purpose or party.

sections.comicCaption: Detective: “Start with the text and the proceeding.” Advocate: “The rules as enacted law: Begin with the rule’s text, read its structure, and use Advisory Committee Notes and relevant legislative history to resolve uncertainty. ”

writtenPractice.prompt: At a grand jury proceeding, counsel objects under 802 and claims Rule 102 makes every protective trial rule applicable. A subpoena also reaches a confidential legal-advice communication.
writtenPractice.analysis: 1101 excludes grand jury proceedings from ordinary evidence-rule application while retaining privilege. 102’s interpretive purposes do not override that scope rule. The privileged communication therefore needs an applicable privilege analysis even though the ordinary hearsay objection may not control.
writtenPractice.variation: Move the same offers into a federal jury trial and identify the changed scope.

sections.title: Foundations review & the coherence of evidence law
sections.tagline: One item can trigger several rules.

points.title: Coverage
points.text: Review foundations, relevance, prejudice, character, impeachment, witnesses, and experts. Explain the legal purpose and limits of each rule.

points.title: Issue sequence
points.text: For each item identify purpose, materiality, rule-specific conditions, prejudice, and procedure. Prior convictions used for substantive propensity and for impeachment are distinct theories with distinct restrictions.

points.title: Policy without shortcuts
points.text: Consider whether the rule’s reliability or institutional rationale fits the facts. Explain both the justification for the rule and its limits.

sections.example: An expert offers an unsupported identity opinion. The prosecutor also offers a similar old conviction as “knowledge” and impeachment if the accused testifies. Write separate analyses for 702, 404(b), 403, and 609 rather than one general fairness conclusion.
tips: State the precise offered purpose and identify the facts needed for this rule’s foundation.
Change one fact in the worked example and explain which requirement changes the result.

terms.definition: Identifying each separate admissibility theory raised by the facts.
The consequential fact the evidence is offered to prove.
Evaluation of a rule’s rationale without substituting it for the governing test.

sections.comicCaption: Detective: “One item can trigger several rules.” Advocate: “Identify relevance, exclusions, and the proper purpose.”

writtenPractice.prompt: A burglary prosecution offers an old similar theft, a shaky eyewitness identification, and a technical expert whose technique lacks explanation. The accused may testify. Outline the independent decisions without discussing hearsay.
writtenPractice.analysis: For the old act identify substantive 404(b) purpose and 403; if a conviction is used for impeachment, separately apply 609’s category, date, and defendant balance. For the identification assess personal knowledge and credibility. For the expert establish 702 qualification, helpfulness, sufficient data, methodology, and application. Preserve objections and consider 105.
writtenPractice.variation: Choose one changed fact for each item that improves admissibility, and one that weakens it.

sections.title: Final review: the complete admissibility argument
sections.tagline: Follow the statement from source to jury.

points.title: Evidence analysis sequence
points.text: For a document or opinion, work through relevance and prejudice, authentication, contents proof, hearsay layers, the applicable exceptions, constitutional limits, and privilege. A successful answer to one question does not decide the others.

points.title: Exam preparation
points.text: Practice explaining why a tempting alternative fails, then write a short rule-application-conclusion for each disputed item.

points.title: Policy review
points.text: Compare the reasons for privilege with the costs of excluding relevant information. Identify the scope, exceptions, and waiver rules before reaching a conclusion.

sections.example: A routine lab file contains an absent analyst’s signed conclusions. A substitute expert relies on it. Ask about identity, record foundation, human versus machine assertions, every hearsay layer, truth dependence, testimonial purpose, and the defendant’s cross-examination opportunity.
tips: State the precise offered purpose and identify the facts needed for this rule’s foundation.
Change one fact in the worked example and explain which requirement changes the result.

terms.definition: An admissibility requirement not resolved by satisfying another rule.
A specific presentation of proposed evidence, purpose, and foundation.
A separate but connected treatment of every rule triggered by one item.

sections.comicCaption: Detective: “Follow the statement from source to jury.” Advocate: “Evidence analysis sequence: For a document or opinion, work through relevance and prejudice, authentication, contents proof, hearsay layers, the applicable exceptions, constitutional limits, and privilege. ”

writtenPractice.prompt: A prosecutor offers an exported lab file with nested human assertions, a substitute opinion, and an accidentally produced legal memo. Write a separate paragraph for each independent objection.
writtenPractice.analysis: The lab file needs authentication and any applicable contents proof. Each human assertion requires its hearsay route; expert reliance and basis disclosure differ. Smith requires truth-use analysis and, for testimonial assertions, confrontation. The legal memo requires governing privilege law and any 502 waiver analysis. None is resolved by merely finding the file relevant.
writtenPractice.variation: Replace a nested assertion with an actual observation by the testifying expert, then explain which barriers remain.

cases.name: United States v. Bello
cases.facts: In a prosecution for a prison assault, the court noticed that the prison lay within federal territorial jurisdiction.
cases.issue: Could the jurisdictional location be judicially noticed?
cases.holding: The notice was permissible on the reliable materials presented; the conviction was affirmed.
cases.reasoning: The location functioned as an adjudicative fact. Rule 201 safeguards applied, including the criminal jury’s freedom not to accept it.
cases.trap: An element-related fact is not automatically beyond notice, but a criminal jury cannot be bound to accept the noticed fact.

cases.name: Huddleston v. United States
cases.facts: A defendant denied knowing that goods were stolen. The government offered his related dealings with suspicious goods.
cases.issue: Must the judge personally find the other act occurred before admission under Rule 404(b)?
cases.holding: No. Sufficient evidence for the jury’s conditional finding satisfied Rule 104(b).
cases.reasoning: The Court relied on a proper purpose, relevant connecting proof, Rule 403, and available limiting instructions as safeguards.
cases.trap: Do not confuse the jury-sufficiency screen with a judge’s independent Rule 104(a) finding.

cases.name: Old Chief v. United States
cases.facts: The accused offered to admit qualifying felony status, but the prosecution introduced the inflammatory name and nature of his prior offense.
cases.issue: How should that adequate alternative affect Rule 403?
cases.holding: Admitting the full conviction record for the status element was an abuse of discretion in these circumstances.
cases.reasoning: The admission proved the legal status with much less risk of improper propensity reasoning. The prior offense’s narrative supplied little additional legitimate value.
cases.trap: This is not a general command to accept every stipulation or abandon coherent event-based proof.

cases.name: United States v. Caldwell
cases.facts: In a firearm-possession prosecution, prior firearm convictions were offered for knowledge and intent and addressed separately as impeachment.
cases.issue: Did the stated purposes justify the prior-conviction evidence?
cases.holding: The court vacated the conviction, rejecting the inadequately supported other-act theory and addressing errors in the impeachment analysis.
cases.reasoning: The actual-possession dispute and the risk of propensity required a specific chain of reasoning and meaningful balancing, not a purpose label.
cases.trap: Rule 404(b) and Rule 609 have different jobs. Success or failure under one does not mechanically decide the other.

cases.name: United States v. Myers
cases.facts: The prosecution used another bank robbery to identify the defendant as the robber in the charged event.
cases.issue: Were the similarities distinctive enough for the identity inference?
cases.holding: The similarities did not adequately support signature-style identity evidence; the conviction was reversed on the errors discussed.
cases.reasoning: Shared commonplace robbery features lacked the unusual combination necessary for the proposed inference.
cases.trap: Compare differences as well as similarities. A generic method is not a fingerprint.

cases.name: Michelson v. United States
cases.facts: A bribery defendant called reputation witnesses; prosecutors tested their knowledge by asking about an earlier arrest.
cases.issue: Could the court permit that inquiry into the basis of reputation testimony?
cases.holding: The Court upheld the controlled cross-examination and affirmed the conviction.
cases.reasoning: The question tested the reputation witnesses’ familiarity with the community reputation, under judicial safeguards and a good-faith basis.
cases.trap: The case predates the Federal Rules. Use current Rules 404 and 405 for the modern framework; the question was not substantive proof of the prior accusation.

cases.name: Babcock v. General Motors Corp.
cases.facts: A product-liability case disputed whether a driver had used his seat belt; witnesses described his consistent seat-belt use.
cases.issue: Could that routine support an inference about the accident trip?
cases.holding: The court upheld admission of the habit evidence and affirmed the judgment.
cases.reasoning: Specific regular conduct supplied more focused proof than a general assertion that the driver was safety-conscious.
cases.trap: Rule 406 can operate without an eyewitness to the disputed occasion; the foundation must still establish a real habit.

cases.name: United States v. Dawson
cases.facts: Defendants wanted to question agents about prior judicial credibility findings. The court clarified its earlier discussion on rehearing.
cases.issue: Did Rule 608(b) categorically prohibit the proposed questions?
cases.holding: No. Permission remained within the trial judge’s discretion; the convictions remained affirmed because any error was harmless.
cases.reasoning: Asking a question differs from introducing the prior ruling as extrinsic proof of untruthful character. Confusion, weak significance, and wasted time may justify limits.
cases.trap: The opinion does not require every prior credibility ruling to be aired. Analyze both the proposed question and its purpose.

cases.name: Luce v. United States
cases.facts: After an adverse preliminary impeachment ruling, the accused did not testify.
cases.issue: Could he obtain review of the threatened Rule 609 use anyway?
cases.holding: No; the defendant had to testify to preserve that claim.
cases.reasoning: Without testimony and actual impeachment, the reviewing court could not reliably evaluate context, the ruling’s effect, or harmlessness.
cases.trap: This holding concerns the specific Rule 609 issue, not every possible pretrial ruling.

cases.name: Ohler v. United States
cases.facts: The accused introduced her prior conviction on direct examination after an adverse pretrial ruling.
cases.issue: Could she then challenge its admission on appeal?
cases.holding: No. Introducing the conviction herself forfeited that appellate challenge.
cases.reasoning: A party who introduces the evidence cannot ordinarily complain about its admission; the tactical choice did not create an exception.
cases.trap: Distinguish a preserved objection followed by the opponent’s impeachment from choosing to introduce the conviction first.

cases.name: Ladd v. Bowers Trucking
cases.facts: A passenger with a memory gap based his collision account on a dream months afterward.
cases.issue: Did the dream-based account establish personal knowledge?
cases.holding: The court affirmed exclusion and summary judgment on this record.
cases.reasoning: The majority distinguished recalling a dream from recalling perception of the event. Mere presence did not fill that foundation. Complex injury causation also required expert proof.
cases.trap: Utah law illustration; the court did not categorically decide that a dream can never restore an actual memory.

cases.name: Travelers v. Ocean Reef Charters
cases.facts: An insurer argued that the absence of a professional captain caused a yacht’s hurricane loss; its expert had been disclosed only for rebuttal.
cases.issue: Could lay observations and a rebuttal-only expert establish the hypothetical captain’s preventive actions?
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment after the insurer failed to provide the necessary affirmative expert proof.
cases.reasoning: Predicting professional storm responses required specialized maritime knowledge. Lay perceptions were not a substitute, and the court did not have to redesignate the expert.
cases.trap: Separate 701/702 classification from civil expert-disclosure procedure.

cases.name: People v. McDonald
cases.facts: Identification was central and disputed; the defense offered a psychologist on perception and memory without endorsing any particular witness.
cases.issue: Could the court exclude the expert simply as invading the jury’s role?
cases.holding: Exclusion was prejudicial error in these circumstances.
cases.reasoning: Specialized explanation can correct misconceptions about identification while leaving credibility and identity to jurors.
cases.trap: California law illustration, not a requirement that every identification case admit an expert.

cases.name: State v. Batangan
cases.facts: A psychologist’s testimony in a child-abuse prosecution implicitly endorsed the complainant’s truthfulness.
cases.issue: May expertise be used to vouch for this witness?
cases.holding: The conviction was vacated and the matter remanded.
cases.reasoning: General explanation of unfamiliar behavior can help; a conclusion that the particular allegation is true usurps credibility assessment.
cases.trap: Hawaii law illustration; distinguish education about behavior from credibility vouching.

cases.name: Diaz v. United States
cases.facts: A defendant denied knowing about concealed drugs; an expert testified that most couriers know what they transport.
cases.issue: Did the group-level opinion violate 704(b)?
cases.holding: The Court held this testimony did not violate 704(b).
cases.reasoning: Most leaves room for exceptions and did not resolve this defendant’s actual knowledge.
cases.trap: Not blanket admissibility under 702 or 403; a proposition covering all people in the defendant’s circumstances can raise a different 704(b) problem.

cases.name: Kumho Tire v. Carmichael
cases.facts: A tire-failure expert attributed a blowout to a defect using a visual/tactile inspection; the defense challenged reliability.
cases.issue: Does gatekeeping apply to technical, experience-based expertise?
cases.holding: Yes; the Court upheld the district court’s exclusion in these circumstances.
cases.reasoning: Reliability applies to all specialized knowledge, with flexible factors tailored to the task and method.
cases.trap: Do not confuse qualification with validated application or demand a uniform laboratory checklist for every discipline.

cases.name: United States v. Ince
cases.facts: After a witness again failed to recall an alleged confession, the prosecution introduced an officer’s account of her earlier unsworn accusation as impeachment.
cases.issue: Was the nominal impeachment an acceptable way to get the accusation before the jury?
cases.holding: The conviction was reversed because the highly prejudicial purported impeachment was improperly admitted.
cases.reasoning: The witness supplied little affirmative testimony to impeach; the accusation’s powerful substantive impact outweighed its limited impeachment value.
cases.trap: 607 permits impeaching one’s own witness but does not create a hearsay-laundering entitlement.

cases.name: Bourjaily v. United States
cases.facts: Recorded negotiations described a friend joining a drug purchase, and the defendant appeared with cash at the arranged transaction.
cases.issue: How are conspiracy foundation facts assessed?
cases.holding: The Court approved preponderance factfinding under 104(a) and consideration of the statement.
cases.reasoning: The statement and surrounding transaction evidence supported the foundational determination.
cases.trap: Use today’s 801(d)(2) text: the statement cannot by itself establish conspiracy or participation. The case’s pre-Crawford confrontation analysis is historical.

cases.name: Williamson v. United States
cases.facts: An arrested courier’s account mixed admissions of his own conduct with assertions implicating another person.
cases.issue: Does 804(b)(3) admit the whole confession because some of it is against interest?
cases.holding: No; the Court required attention to individual self-inculpatory statements and remanded.
cases.reasoning: A narrative’s overall disserving character does not establish that every included assertion is reliably against the speaker’s interest.
cases.trap: Context matters; even a seemingly neutral statement may be self-inculpatory in context. Criminal corroboration requirements remain.

cases.name: Crawford v. Washington
cases.facts: The prosecution used a wife’s recorded police-interrogation account when she did not testify and the defendant had no chance to cross-examine her.
cases.issue: Could judicial findings of reliability justify this testimonial statement?
cases.holding: No; the Court reversed.
cases.reasoning: The Clause protects confrontation rather than replacing it with a judge’s reliability assessment.
cases.trap: Analyze truth use and testimonial status first; not every out-of-court statement is testimonial.

cases.name: Smith v. Arizona
cases.facts: A substitute expert relied on an absent analyst’s factual assertions to identify seized substances.
cases.issue: Are the assertions nontruth evidence merely because described as an opinion’s basis?
cases.holding: No; truth-dependent basis assertions are offered for their truth. The Court remanded for further analysis.
cases.reasoning: The opinion depends on the absent analyst being correct, so a basis-only label cannot avoid the constitutional inquiry.
cases.trap: The Court did not hold every laboratory statement testimonial. That question remains a separate inquiry.

cases.name: Samia v. United States
cases.facts: At a joint trial, a nontestifying defendant’s confession referred to the other participant neutrally, with a limiting instruction.
cases.issue: Did this modified confession violate the codefendant’s confrontation rights?
cases.holding: The Court found no violation under the circumstances presented.
cases.reasoning: The confession did not directly identify the nonconfessing defendant and was accompanied by an appropriate instruction.
cases.trap: Bruton remains relevant to direct naming; Gray’s obvious-deletion circumstances are different.

cases.name: United States v. Zhyltsou
cases.facts: The government introduced a social-network profile bearing the defendant’s identity without sufficient proof he created or controlled it.
cases.issue: Did the page’s contents alone adequately establish the claimed authorship?
cases.holding: The conviction was vacated and the case remanded for retrial.
cases.reasoning: A page’s appearance is distinct from its attribution to the defendant; the proponent lacked the necessary linking evidence.
cases.trap: A distinctive or corroborated digital record can be authenticated; the opinion does not prohibit internet evidence generally.

cases.name: Jaffee v. Redmond
cases.facts: After a police shooting, the officer obtained therapy from a licensed clinical social worker; civil plaintiffs sought the counseling communications.
cases.issue: Does federal common law recognize a psychotherapist-patient privilege covering this counseling?
cases.holding: Yes; confidential therapeutic communications were protected.
cases.reasoning: Effective treatment depends on trust and confidentiality, supporting recognition under 501’s reason-and-experience approach.
cases.trap: The Court rejected routine case-by-case evidentiary balancing; distinguish privilege from ethical disclosure obligations and questions left unresolved.

cases.name: Carmody v. Board of Trustees of the University of Illinois
cases.facts: A legal memo slipped through a reviewed production. Counsel sought return upon learning the opponent would use it, then followed up and moved promptly.
cases.issue: Did the disclosure waive attorney-client privilege under 502(b)?
cases.holding: No; the court upheld protection on the established facts.
cases.reasoning: The disclosure was inadvertent, preventive review was reasonable though imperfect, and corrective efforts were prompt and reasonable.
cases.trap: A privilege stamp alone does not establish all three conditions; delay is assessed against when the error became known.
